enrichment.short_title: Tenant's claim for post-expiry rent loss fails where Middlesbrough offices were unlettable despite admitted repair breaches
key_facts: Marchday claimed damages from BT for breach of repairing, cleansing and decorating covenants in a 1976 underlease of upper floors and car parking at Corporation House, Middlesbrough, which expired on 25 March 2000.

BT admitted breaches and agreed remedial works cost £348,830.25; Marchday additionally claimed about £808,319 for lost rent, insurance and service charges over 19 months while remedial works and re-letting were allegedly delayed.
The demised premises were not re-let until Garland took leases in 2003 at higher per-square-foot rates after extensive refurbishment rebranding the building as Centre North East.

Expert evidence showed Middlesbrough was oversupplied with poor-quality 1970s office stock and competition from Teesdale new builds; remedial works alone would have delayed re-letting by only about five weeks.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Technology and Construction Court on quantum of damages after admission of repairing covenant breaches at lease expiry.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Marchday for £407,522.80 comprising agreed repair damages (net of service charge rebate), interest from 1 October 2000 at 8% simple, but refusal of disputed consequential loss claims.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tenant admits breach of repairing covenants at lease expiry, consequential claims for lost rent, insurance and service charges depend on proving the premises could have been re-let earlier if delivered up in repair; overwhelming market evidence that oversupplied, obsolete office stock in Middlesbrough was unlettable until full refurbishment defeated that claim, and a tenant cannot recover loss attributable to its own upgrading works or other parties' breaches.
legal_issues: Whether the demised premises could have been re-let immediately from 25 March 2000 if delivered up in repair
What rental value and period of loss were recoverable for admitted breaches
Appropriate date and rate of interest on agreed repair damages

enrichment.short_title: Bedfordia fails to quash Huntingdonshire Local Plan refusal to allocate Eaton Socon site despite Inspector's housing recommendation

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Bedfordia sought to challenge adoption of the Huntingdonshire Local Plan Alteration after the council declined to accept an Inspector's recommendation to allocate part of Bedfordia Fields at Eaton Socon for housing.
The Inspector had carried the site through a sustainability assessment under PPG3 but the council gave greater weight to visual harm and countryside loss, supported by substantial public opposition.
Bedfordia argued other sites (Buckden, Fenstanton, Ramsey St. Mary, Yaxley) should have been deleted before its site and that the council lacked an open mind.
The court heard the case immediately after Fairfield Partnership v Huntingdonshire DC, where the converse complaint (following the Inspector) had also failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 287 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash adoption of a local plan alteration.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; council's refusal to allocate the site and its reasons held lawful.
enrichment.ratio: A local planning authority must give adequate reasons for departing from an Inspector's recommendation but retains the last word on weighting material planning considerations; refusing allocation where visual harm to countryside outweighs PPG3 sustainability factors, where surplus housing land exists, and where village sites with planning permission were retained for practical reasons, is not Wednesbury unreasonable nor procedurally defective.
legal_issues: Whether Huntingdonshire had adequate reasons for rejecting the Inspector's allocation recommendation
Whether deletion of other village sites and preference for Yaxley over Bedfordia Fields was unlawful
Whether the council had a closed mind to the Inspector's recommendation

enrichment.short_title: Qualified privilege struck out over Daily Mail articles blaming DCI Miller for Hamilton sex inquiry 'shambles'
key_facts: Detective Chief Inspector Christopher Miller sued Associated Newspapers over September 2001 Daily Mail and Evening Standard articles criticising the Metropolitan Police investigation of false indecent assault allegations against Neil and Christine Hamilton.
The defendants pleaded justification and qualified privilege; the claimant sought to strike out privilege under CPR Part 24.

Journalists relied on confidential interim progress report material from Acting Commander John Yates and internal police sources, without approaching Miller, while criminal and disciplinary processes were unresolved.
The defendants conceded an amended justification plea was viable but the court struck out qualified privilege on the pleaded facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to strike out qualified privilege defence in libel proceedings; partial success on justification plea amendment.
enrichment.outcome: Qualified privilege defence struck out; defendants to pay claimant's costs of that issue; justification to proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Under Reynolds, publication of defamatory allegations attributing incompetence to a specific officer based on a partial, secondhand account of a confidential interim internal review, while investigations and disciplinary proceedings remained live, does not satisfy the objective social or moral duty test; reliable sources and general public interest in police efficiency do not create a right to publish unverified blame, and opinions of journalists or unnamed officers are not privileged information of requisite status.
legal_issues: Whether Reynolds qualified privilege applied to publication of allegations about DCI Miller's conduct
Whether interim confidential police review material justified premature public attribution of blame
Whether the defence should be struck out under CPR Part 24

enrichment.short_title: Newcastle Grainger Town CPO challenge dismissed as merits-only claim with no error of law
key_facts: Mr Mohammed and Mr Offord challenged confirmation of a compulsory purchase order affecting shop and flat units at Sunderland Street needed for phase 4B of Newcastle City Council's Grainger Town regeneration scheme.
Claimants argued development was not comprehensive, existing businesses were viable under the UDP, and confirmation disproportionately interfered with Article 1 Protocol rights.
The Inspector had considered and rejected these arguments, finding provisional development agreements and funding showed strong likelihood of comprehensive planned development.
Claimants failed to comply with CPR practice direction, produced no skeleton, and sought adjournment due to Mr Offord's illness; Mr Mohammed did not appear.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Challenge to Secretary of State's confirmation of a compulsory purchase order; adjournment refused.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no conceivable error of law or procedure identified.
enrichment.ratio: Judicial review of CPO confirmation is confined to errors of law or procedure; arguments that the Inspector should have preferred refurbishment over compulsory acquisition, that development lacked comprehensiveness, or that Article 1 Protocol rights were infringed are merits-based planning judgments lawfully made by the Inspector and accepted by the Secretary of State, and cannot be re-argued without identifying a legal flaw.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State erred in confirming the CPO
Whether Article 1 Protocol required withdrawal of the order at phase 4B
Whether an adjournment should be granted

enrichment.short_title: Legal aid franchise refusal actionable under Race Relations Act s.12 but not as employment under s.4
key_facts: Ms Patterson, sole principal of Patterson Sebastian & Co, alleged race discrimination in the Legal Services Commission's handling of her legal aid franchise application under the Community Legal Service accreditation scheme.
The Employment Tribunal held no jurisdiction under section 4 or section 12; the EAT reversed on both grounds.

A three-year General Civil Contract payable on architect-style certificates was the contractual mechanism; the sole practitioner was not personally obliged to perform contracted legal work under LAFQAS franchise representative and supervisor roles.
Franchise accreditation enabled publicly funded work and conferred status via the franchise logo, distinct from merely selecting a solicitor to perform services.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on preliminary jurisdiction issues in an Employment Tribunal race discrimination claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on section 4 (no employment jurisdiction); appeal dismissed on section 12 (qualifying body jurisdiction upheld).
enrichment.ratio: A sole practitioner's three-year Community Legal Service contract is not a contract whose dominant purpose is personal execution of work or labour within section 78, because the contractor may delegate performance to personnel and approved representatives and franchise representative/supervisor roles are replaceable without Commission consent; but granting LAFQAS franchise accreditation is conferring an authorisation that facilitates engagement in the solicitor's profession within section 12, even though the practitioner is not in the Commission's employment.
legal_issues: Whether franchise discrimination falls within section 4 employment field
Whether franchise grant is an authorisation or qualification under section 12
How section 12 applies to sole practitioners and partnerships

enrichment.short_title: £75,000 Colonial Finance retention was non-reducing until last delivery, then used to meet customer claims
key_facts: After Kingsway Scotland and KSC Trading entered administration, Colonial Finance agreed by letter of 1 September 2000 to withdraw termination of finance facilities subject to retaining £75,000 against future customer claims under indemnified credit sale agreements.
Administrators argued the retention should reduce as each post-September claim was met; Colonial argued it remained at £75,000 until limitation expired.
The deputy judge held a running £75,000 float reducing from 21 February 2001 when business ceased, producing a money judgment for about £34,270.83.
Outstanding furniture orders were fulfilled until the last delivery on 15 March 2001; Colonial had been offsetting claims against sums due to Kingsway before that date.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issue determination on construction of September 2000 finance continuation letter in administrators' claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; retention non-reducing until 15 March 2001, then applied to meet customer claims with balance due 15 March 2007.
enrichment.ratio: Construing the September 2000 letter in its factual matrix, Colonial was entitled to maintain a £75,000 reserve while interim payments continued until the last delivery eliminated future Kingsway receipts; only from that date, when security against indemnity claims became necessary, did the retention operate as a fund to be reduced by customer claims, with any balance accounted for at the end of the limitation period.
legal_issues: Whether the £75,000 retention reduced from 1 September 2000 or only after business ceased
When Colonial could withhold sums from payments due to Kingsway
Financial consequences of the contractual construction

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors' failure to advise on implemented CPOs warrants retrial on whether Patel would have bought Twyford Tip site
key_facts: Mr Patel contracted through Asiansky companies to buy Twyford Tip West from Brent Council for an Asian Centre development, but about 40% of the site was subject to implemented DoT compulsory purchase orders with Notices to Treat and Enter.

Respondent solicitors failed from August 1992 to warn that implementation gave the DoT indefinite possession rights and did not properly advise on the October 1992 DoT letter of comfort before exchange on 19 October 1992.
The judge underestimated negligence and found Patel would have proceeded anyway, relying on Brent to resolve CPO issues with the DoT.
Brent had no power to affect DoT's use of implemented CPO rights; Patel also bought the British Pavilion for the scheme without planning permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from trial dismissing professional negligence claim except nominal contract damages; permission granted by Pill LJ.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; order below set aside; causation to be retried by a different High Court judge; security for costs arrangements varied.
enrichment.ratio: A conveyancer who from August 1992 knew CPOs covered 40% of the purchase land and had been implemented by Notices to Treat and Enter was in stark breach of duty in failing to warn the client he would not obtain vacant possession and in not explaining the letter of comfort; whether the client would still have exchanged is a causation question that cannot be resolved on the inadequate breach analysis at first instance, and confidence that the selling council could sort matters with the DoT is not a sustainable basis for finding no loss where the council had no legal power over the acquiring authority.
legal_issues: Extent of solicitors' breach in advising on CPO implementation and letter of comfort
Whether Patel would have exchanged contracts if properly advised (causation)
Whether reliance on implemented CPOs was an illegitimate change of case

enrichment.short_title: HGCRA s.111 requires payment on architect's certificate without withholding notice — pay now, litigate later

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Clients disputed about £27,000 of a seventh interim certificate (£44,000 plus VAT) under an ASI standard form contract for cottage building works.
No effective section 111 withholding notice was served before the prescribed period; builders sought summary judgment for the balance.
Under the contract, payment follows the architect's certificate, not verification of actual work done; certificates are not conclusive of ultimate liability.
Clients argued work was not done, duplicated or wrongly charged as extras, so no sum was due and section 111 did not apply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court summary judgment application on preliminary construction of section 111(1).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; clients must pay certified sum now but may pursue adjudication or proceedings if they overpaid.
enrichment.ratio: Section 111(1) is a cash-flow mechanism, not a rule making certificates conclusive: where an ASI contract defines the sum due by the architect's certificate and the due date by certificate date, a party may not withhold payment after the final date without an effective withholding notice, even if the certificate includes disputed items, but failure to withhold does not prevent later correction in subsequent certificates, adjudication or litigation — the mischief addressed is wrongful withholding by paying parties, not final allocation of liability.
legal_issues: Whether absence of a withholding notice precludes defending on basis work was not done
Wide versus narrow construction of section 111(1)
Relationship between certified sums and ultimate contractual liability

enrichment.short_title: Ivorian RDR supporter refused permission to appeal asylum refusal after failed 2002 coup

statutes_considered.title: Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: Ivorian appellant claimed persecution as a Muslim northern-origin supporter of the RDR party following arrests and detentions in 2000 and 2001.
Adjudicator found limited government interest in the appellant, doubted he was Muslim, and that situation had improved after President Gbagbo's election.

After a failed coup on 19 September 2002 the Immigration Appeal Tribunal granted leave to appeal on changed country conditions but dismissed the appeal, applying Oleed on reassessing country evidence.
Tribunal held risk factors were not supported by adjudicator's credibility findings; State Department and Human Rights Watch materials did not show low-level RDR supporters faced persecution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from dismissal by the Immigration Appeal Tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: Even if the Tribunal misapplied Oleed in treating fresh country evidence on the Ivory Coast coup as requiring the adjudicator's determination to be plainly wrong before reconsideration, dismissal was justified because credibility findings — including that authorities had no particular interest in this low-level RDR supporter and that he was not shown to be Muslim — remained fatal, and post-coup country evidence did not establish that such supporters faced persecution.
legal_issues: Whether Oleed governs Tribunal reconsideration of country conditions on appeal
Whether changed circumstances after September 2002 coup warranted asylum
Adequacy of adjudicator's credibility findings

enrichment.short_title: Service of Form E validly commenced drug trafficking cash forfeiture and stopped section 42 detention clock

statutes_considered.title: Magistrates' Courts (Detention and Forfeiture of Drug Trafficking Cash) Rules 1991

key_facts: Claimant was stopped at Waterloo with about £87,000 in European currencies in footwear and luggage; cash was seized and detained under section 42 of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994.
Customs served Form E on the magistrates' court on 10 April 2002 seeking forfeiture under section 43, which under section 42(7) stopped the detention clock beyond 3 May 2002.
Claimant argued serving Form E alone did not constitute a valid forfeiture application without compliance with Rule 9(2) fixing and notifying a hearing date.
After adjournments and an unsuccessful earlier judicial review, the district judge ordered forfeiture on 5 March 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review to quash magistrates' court forfeiture order; permission granted by Moses J.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; valid section 43 application and lawful continued detention upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An application for forfeiture under section 43 is made when Form E is served on the justices' chief executive under Rule 9, which stops the section 42 detention clock under section 42(7) even before a hearing date is fixed; procedural defects in notifying the hearing date do not render subsequent forfeiture proceedings a nullity, and in this case the claimant received notice of fixed hearing dates for forfeiture proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether service of Form E alone amounted to a section 43 application
Whether Rule 9(2) compliance was mandatory for valid forfeiture proceedings
Whether continued detention after 3 May 2002 was lawful
